findings.summary: Page titles lag their content by about one page, so a learner navigating by title lands on the page after the material.
findings.evidence: Page 4 is titled "Capture Traps & @ Sugar", but the capture-trap sections ("1. Cells Hold Names, Not Values", "fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]") and "4. @ Is Literally Rebinding" all sit on page 3; page 4 opens on "5. Minimal Wrapper" and runs into functools.wraps. Same offset on pages 3, 5, 6 and 8.
findings.fix: Retitle each page after the material it actually opens with (page 3 "Closures & Capture Traps", page 4 "@ Sugar & Wrapper Basics", page 5 "wraps & Argument Forwarding", page 6 "Forwarding & Decorator Factories", page 8 "Stack Order & Practice"), or move the section breaks so each page starts on its titled topic.

findings.summary: Claim that functools.wraps can raise AttributeError on builtins/C functions is false for missing attributes since Python 3.2.
findings.evidence: "On builtins or C functions it can raise `AttributeError`"
findings.fix: Replace with: update_wrapper silently skips attributes the wrapped object lacks (try/except AttributeError since Python 3.2); on builtins you simply get incomplete metadata (e.g. no __doc__/__qualname__ copied), not an exception.

findings.summary: The described failure mode of a bare `@repeat` is wrong — it raises TypeError at the first call, never reaching `range(n)`.
findings.evidence: "`@repeat` binds your function to `n` — no error at that line" / "It explodes later inside `range(n)`, far from the cause"
findings.fix: State the real behaviour: `f = repeat(f)` makes `f` the inner `deco`, so `f()` raises `TypeError: deco() missing 1 required positional argument: 'fn'` — matching the 'Silent Four' entry on page 10.

findings.fix: Render the factory example as one continuous code block in a single column, or give the continuation panel an explicit label (e.g. "Factory Skeleton, cont.") so the dangling indentation reads as a continuation.

When Order Bites", alongside the existing "`@staticmethod` and `@classmethod` outermost" bullet; on page 7 state only that `@classmethod` returns a descriptor rather than a plain function.

findings.summary: Repeats the false claim that closure-based decorators are more pickle-friendly than class-based ones.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["closure decorator","terse, pickle-friendlier"]
findings.fix: Change to "terse, no extra type"; note that class-instance decorators are the picklable option since local functions are not picklable.

findings.summary: "Never add the parens" is stated as absolute but decorator factories require them, as the handbook itself later teaches.
findings.evidence: "Decorators need the object, so never add the parens."
findings.fix: Qualify: a plain decorator takes the function object (`@deco`); parens mean you are calling a decorator *factory* (`@repeat(3)`), which must return a decorator.

findings.summary: Listing "gets returned" as a necessary condition for a closure is wrong — the cell is created by referencing the free variable, regardless of whether the inner function escapes.
findings.evidence: "Three conditions: nested def, reads an outer name, gets returned"
findings.fix: Cut the third condition (or reword to "usually escapes the outer call"): any nested def reading an enclosing name has `__closure__` populated, returned or not.

findings.summary: "Captured cells" is used as an explanatory term one page before cells are introduced.
findings.evidence: Page 2, "5. Nested Defs Are Fresh": "New function object, new captured cells, each time" — cells are first shown on page 3 ("5. Open The Cells", `add5.__closure__[0].cell_contents  # 5`).
findings.fix: On page 2 write "new captured bindings, each time" and keep the word "cells" for page 3, where `__closure__` and `cell_contents` define it.

findings.summary: "Byte-for-byte identical" overstates the desugaring — the decorator expression is evaluated before the def and the name is never bound to the undecorated function.
findings.evidence: "# byte-for-byte identical to:" ... "f = deco(f)      # runs right after the def"
findings.fix: Say "semantically equivalent to" and note that in the `@` form the decorator expression is evaluated first and `f` is only ever bound to the result.

findings.summary: Wrapper code uses `*a, **kw` for two pages before the collect/unpack semantics are taught.
findings.evidence: Page 3 shows "def wrapper(*a, **kw): return fn(*a, **kw)" (repeated on page 4's "5. Minimal Wrapper"), but "1. Collect, Then Unpack" — "def line: tuple of positionals / call line: unpacks the tuple" — appears only on page 5.
findings.fix: Add a one-line gloss under the first minimal wrapper on page 3 — "`*a, **kw` collects every argument on the def line and unpacks it again on the call line; full detail on page 5" — or move the "Collect, Then Unpack" table ahead of the minimal wrapper.

findings.summary: Two of the three examples credited to PEP 614 were already legal decorator syntax before Python 3.9.
findings.evidence: "Since PEP 614: `@registry[name]`, `@obj.method`, `@make_deco(x)`"
findings.fix: Keep only `@registry[name]` (and other arbitrary expressions) under PEP 614 / Python 3.9+; the old grammar `'@' dotted_name ['(' arglist ')']` already allowed `@obj.method` and `@make_deco(x)`.

findings.summary: The benefit "no metadata loss" is claimed before the reader has been shown that wrappers lose metadata.
findings.evidence: Page 4, "1. Wrapper-Free Decorators": "No wrapper means no metadata loss and no extra frame" — the loss itself is only demonstrated in the next section, "2. Naive Wrappers Erase Identity" (`__name__` → 'wrapper', `__doc__` → None).
findings.fix: Swap the two sections so "Naive Wrappers Erase Identity" comes first, or reword the bullet to "No wrapper at all — nothing to wrap means nothing to fix (see next section)".

findings.summary: Claim that tracebacks read 'wrapper' only when @wraps is missing is wrong — tracebacks use `__code__.co_name`, which wraps never changes.
findings.evidence: "help(), pydoc, Sphinx autodoc, pytest test ids, debugger tracebacks. All of them say 'wrapper' without wraps."
findings.fix: Drop "debugger tracebacks" from the list, or note explicitly that traceback frames always show `wrapper` because wraps copies attributes, not the code object.

findings.summary: The comment showing the output of `print(args, kwargs)` renders the two values as a single tuple.
findings.evidence: "    print(args, kwargs)  # ((1,), {'b': 2})"
findings.fix: Change the comment to `# (1,) {'b': 2}` — print separates the two arguments with a space.

findings.summary: "Descriptor" is used as load-bearing vocabulary but is never defined anywhere in the handbook.
findings.evidence: Page 7: "`@classmethod` returns a descriptor, so it must be outermost"; the earlier "5. The Method Problem" explains the same mechanism only as "loses binding — no `self` arrives" and "unless you implement `__get__`".
findings.fix: Add a one-line definition in "5. The Method Problem": "A descriptor is any object defining `__get__`; that hook is what binds `self` on attribute access."

findings.summary: Attributing a truncated traceback to omitting `from e` is wrong — implicit context chaining still shows the original exception.
findings.evidence: Table row: ["traceback stops at the wrapper","re-raise without `from e`"]
findings.fix: Correct the cause: without `from e` you still get "During handling of the above exception, another exception occurred"; the original is truly lost only with `raise ... from None` or by swallowing the exception. `from e` sets `__cause__` for a cleaner "The above exception was the direct cause" chain.
